nameStory: Winged pigweed gets its name from the distinctive papery wings that develop on its stems as it matures. The 'pigweed' part comes from the old farming tradition of feeding these nutritious plants to pigs, while the 'winged' refers to the thin, membranous ridges that run along the stems like tiny fins.
description: Winged pigweed is an annual herb that grows 1-3 feet tall with a bushy, spreading appearance. It's a member of the amaranth family and develops characteristic papery wings along its stems that make it quite distinctive. The plant produces small, inconspicuous flowers and eventually breaks off at the base to tumble in the wind, earning it the nickname 'plains tumbleweed.' Despite being uncommon in New England with only 12 recorded observations, it's worth knowing since it's such an unusual-looking plant when you do encounter it.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: The most distinctive feature - stems develop thin, papery wings or ridges that you can feel with your fingers, giving them a fluted or ribbed texture unlike most other weeds

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms a rounded, bushy plant that eventually breaks off at the base to tumble like a tumbleweed - you might find detached plants caught against fences or buildings

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, lance-shaped leaves that feel slightly thick and succulent-like to the touch, arranged alternately along the winged stems

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny, greenish flowers clustered along the stems that are easy to miss - no showy petals, just small bumpy clusters that feel slightly rough when rubbed

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Small, round seeds enclosed in papery bracts that make a subtle rattling sound when the dried plant is shaken

habitat: In New England, winged pigweed is typically found in disturbed, sandy soils along roadsides, railway corridors, and waste areas. It prefers well-drained, often poor soils and full sun exposure. Since it's native to the western plains, it's quite rare in our region and most likely to appear where western seeds might have been transported.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge as small rosettes with the characteristic winged stems just beginning to develop. The wings become more pronounced as the plant grows.
seasonality.summer: Plants reach full size with fully developed stem wings and produce their inconspicuous flowers. This is the best time to observe the distinctive winged stem feature.
seasonality.fall: Plants mature and dry out, eventually breaking off at the base to tumble. The papery wings become very pronounced and brittle, and seeds are dispersed.
seasonality.winter: Dried, detached plants may persist as tumbleweeds caught in fences or vegetation. The distinctive winged stems remain visible on these skeletal remains.

funFact: This plant is essentially a living tumbleweed that can travel hundreds of miles from where it grew, spreading seeds as it bounces across the landscape - some individual plants have been tracked rolling for over 1,000 miles across the Great Plains!
confusionNotes: The winged stems make this plant quite distinctive, but young plants without fully developed wings might be confused with other pigweeds or goosefoots. Memory trick: if you can feel papery ridges running along the stem like tiny airplane wings, you've found winged pigweed.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'pigweed,' this plant isn't closely related to the more common pigweeds (Amaranthus species) that most people know. It was recently moved to the genus Dysphania from Cycloloma, so you might see it listed under either name in older field guides.
compareHints: Unlike its Dysphania relatives like Mexican tea (which has a strong, pungent odor when crushed) or clammy goosefoot (which feels sticky), winged pigweed is distinguished by its papery stem wings and lack of strong scent. The other species in this genus have round stems and different textures, making winged pigweed the easiest to identify once you know what to feel for.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its relatives like Mexican tea and Jerusalem oak, clammy goosefoot is much smaller and has the distinctive sticky texture.
Mexican tea differs from its relatives like clammy goosefoot and Jerusalem oak primarily by its much stronger, more pungent smell and its narrow, lance-shaped leaves.
Jerusalem oak stands out from its Dysphania relatives by its deeply cut, almost fern-like leaves - Mexican tea and clammy goosefoot have much simpler, less divided leaves.
